approachQuestion.prompt:
A standout sensor

A line of sensors supplies a read-only random-access array `height`. Adjacent values are unequal, but values farther apart may repeat. Return any index whose value is strictly greater than each existing immediate neighbor. End sensors have just one neighbor; a singleton qualifies. You need not return the global maximum.

Constraints: 1 <= n <= 200000; heights are signed 32-bit integers. Prefer the method with the smallest worst-case number of array probes, then least working memory.

Examples: [3,8,5,7,2] -> 1 or 3; [9,6,2] -> 0; [4] -> 0.
constraints: No global sortedness or single-peak shape is promised.

options.text: Maintain lo=0, hi=n-1. While lo<hi, set mid=floor((lo+hi)/2). If height[mid]<height[mid+1], set lo=mid+1; otherwise set hi=mid. Return lo.
options.feedback: An upward step guarantees a peak on its right before the boundary; a downward step guarantees one on its left including mid. The maintained endpoint slopes preserve a valid peak even with many peaks.

options.text: Use the same slope test recursively on index bounds, returning when the bounds coincide.
options.feedback: This returns a valid peak for every legal array, but recursion stores avoidable frames. An iterative loop retains the same candidates with less memory.

options.text: Scan every sensor, tracking an index of a global maximum, and return it.
options.feedback: A global maximum is a valid peak because adjacent values differ, but probing every sensor loses the requested worst-case efficiency when a slope search can discard intervals.

options.text: Compare midpoint to the first sensor. If larger, discard the left half; otherwise discard the right half; return the remaining index.
options.feedback: For [1,5,3], midpoint 5 is above the first value and this rule retains only index 2, which is not a peak.

feedback.reason: Keep two index bounds. Compare the midpoint with its next neighbor: move the left bound past midpoint on an upward slope, and move the right bound to midpoint on a downward slope. Adjacent inequality removes flat steps. The interval retains a peak until its bounds meet.
details: Keep two index bounds. Compare the midpoint with its next neighbor: move the left bound past midpoint on an upward slope, and move the right bound to midpoint on a downward slope. Adjacent inequality removes flat steps. The interval retains a peak until its bounds meet.

An upward adjacent slope guarantees a peak on the right when endpoints have the stated outside-boundary convention; a downward slope preserves one on the left. The method needs some peak, not the global maximum.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only slope-search, the iterative midpoint/next-neighbor method above. Let n be the length. Random access and fixed-width arithmetic are constant time; no input copies, recursion, or output collection are used. Choose the tightest worst-case pair.
constraints: Use worst-case bounds. Count all working memory including any stack; exclude supplied inputs and the scalar result.

options.text: O(n log(n + 1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: A slope comparison halves the candidate interval without copying values.
details: Comparing midpoint with its next neighbor selects an interval at most half as long. Repeating gives logarithmically many slope tests. Only endpoints, midpoint, and probed values are live; multiple possible peaks do not require a list of candidates.
“O(log(n + 1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The index interval halves and only scalar bounds are stored.
“O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Each slope test discards half the candidate interval instead of walking every reading.
“O(log(n + 1)) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: Only scalar bounds and adjacent midpoint values are needed; the readings are never copied.
“O(n log(n + 1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: There is one constant-time slope comparison per halving step, not a full n-entry scan per step.

methodReveal.title: Follow a slope while preserving a peak
methodReveal.description: Keep two index bounds. Compare the midpoint with its next neighbor: move the left bound past midpoint on an upward slope, and move the right bound to midpoint on a downward slope. Adjacent inequality removes flat steps. The interval retains a peak until its bounds meet.
